chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Sulayman ibn Khalid said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who had money with him that belonged to me, and he stubbornly refused to pay me and swore an oath. Then money of his came to be with me. Should I take it in return for the money I took from him, deny him, and swear an oath against him as he did? He said, 'If he cheated you, do not cheat him, and do not enter into what you accused him of.'

key_terms.أَجْحَدُهُ: I deny him/refuse to pay him

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on taking back money from someone who stubbornly refused to pay you and swore an oath?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between legal reciprocity and ethical conduct, ruling that one should not mirror the debtor's specific vice of *kabr* (stubbornness) and false oath-taking (*huluf*) even if entitled to withhold assets. This reflects the Shia principle of *ihsan* (excellence) in transactions, where the creditor avoids *jahd* (denial) to maintain moral superiority over mere legal right. The hadith emphasizes that while the debt remains valid, the manner of recovery should be free from the hypocrisy of the debtor.
